title: SQL interview classics: joins, aggregation, subqueries and NULLs
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: Join types, GROUP BY and HAVING, NULL three-valued logic, NOT IN vs NOT EXISTS, and the classic questions: second highest salary, duplicates, self-join for managers, anti-join. Queries verified on PostgreSQL 16.
source: PostgreSQL 16 documentation (queries, functions); Use The Index, Luke; LeetCode SQL discussions; Mode and SQLZoo tutorials; Joe Celko on NULL logic

questions.prompt: Match each join form to the rows it produces.

left.text: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE right.id IS NULL

right.text: Only rows with a match on both sides
All left rows, with NULLs in right columns where unmatched
All rows from both sides, matched where possible
Cartesian product: m x n rows
Anti-join: left rows that have no match
A table joined to itself through two aliases
Pairs of rows that happen to have the same row number

questions.explanation: Every outer join is "inner join plus the unmatched rows". The LEFT JOIN + IS NULL idiom is the anti-join; NOT EXISTS is its cleaner, NULL-safe cousin.

questions.prompt: Table employees has 8 rows whose dept_id values are 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3 and NULL. How many rows does SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employees GROUP BY dept_id return?
questions.explanation: GROUP BY treats all NULLs as one group, so the groups are 1, 2, 3 and NULL. (Verified on PostgreSQL.) This differs from equality, where NULL = NULL is not true.

questions.prompt: departments has ids 1, 2, 3, 4 (id 4 is Legal); employees.dept_id values are 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3 and NULL. For SELECT d.name, COUNT(*) FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id GROUP BY d.name, what count is shown next to Legal?
questions.explanation: The unmatched department still produces one null-extended row, and COUNT(*) counts rows, so Legal shows 1. COUNT(e.id) would show 0 because it ignores NULLs. Classic interview trap.

questions.prompt: employees has ids 1 to 8 and manager_id values NULL, 1, 1, 1, 4, 4, 1, 7 (one row has no manager). How many rows does SELECT * FROM employees WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employees) return?
questions.explanation: NOT IN against a list that contains NULL can never be true: id <> NULL is unknown for every id that is not matched. The query returns 0 rows although employees 2, 3, 5, 6 and 8 manage nobody. NOT EXISTS (or filtering manager_id IS NOT NULL) returns the 5 non-managers.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: A condition such as COUNT(*) > 1 must be written in HAVING, not in WHERE.
questions.reason: WHERE is evaluated before GROUP BY, at a point where the aggregates do not exist yet.

whys.a: Correct: R states the logical processing order that forces A.
whys.b: R is the cause of A, so it does explain it.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: Use WHERE to filter input rows (cheaper, can use indexes) and HAVING to filter groups. Row-level conditions placed in HAVING work but do more work.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: In a table of 8 employees where exactly one manager_id is NULL, COUNT(manager_id) returns 8.
questions.reason: COUNT(column) counts only the rows in which that column is not NULL.

whys.a: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.b: A is false, so both-true options are wrong.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: Correct: COUNT(manager_id) is 7 here, while COUNT(*) is 8; R is true.

questions.explanation: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values, COUNT(DISTINCT col) counts distinct non-NULL values. All aggregates except COUNT(*) skip NULLs, and SUM over zero non-NULL rows is NULL.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion (A) and the reason (R), then choose the option that fits.
questions.assertion: NOT EXISTS gives the expected anti-join result even when the correlated column contains NULLs, unlike NOT IN.
questions.reason: PostgreSQL can execute NOT EXISTS as a hash anti join.

whys.a: The anti-join execution strategy is not why NULLs behave differently.
whys.b: Correct: both are true, but R is about performance, not about three-valued logic.
whys.c: R is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.
whys.d: A is true, so this option wrongly calls it false.

questions.explanation: NOT EXISTS only asks whether a matching row exists, so a NULL never poisons the result. NOT IN (subquery) returns no rows if the subquery yields any NULL.

questions.prompt: Complete the NULL rules by dragging the words into the blanks.
questions.text: `manager_id = NULL` evaluates to {1}, never to true. WHERE keeps a row only when its predicate is {2}, so that filter returns no rows. The correct test for missing values is `manager_id IS {3}`.
questions.explanation: SQL uses three-valued logic: TRUE, FALSE, UNKNOWN. NOT UNKNOWN is still UNKNOWN, which is why x <> 1 also drops rows where x is NULL.

questions.prompt: Table employees(id, name, salary) holds salaries 150, 120, 120, 100, 90, 90, 80, 70. Write one query that returns the second highest distinct salary (120 for this data).

checks.label: removes the top value with a subquery on MAX, DENSE_RANK, or DISTINCT + OFFSET

questions.model:
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees
WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);
questions.explanation: Also valid: SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1, or DENSE_RANK() in a subquery. Without DISTINCT/DENSE_RANK the tie at 120 would break the OFFSET and ROW_NUMBER variants. Verified on PostgreSQL.

questions.prompt: Table users(id, email). Write a query that lists every email that occurs more than once together with how many times, as column cnt.
questions.model:
SELECT email, COUNT(*) AS cnt
FROM users
GROUP BY email
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;
questions.explanation: A window function (COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY email)) in a subquery also works. To delete the extras keep MIN(id) per email.

questions.prompt: Table employees(id, name, manager_id) where manager_id refers to employees.id. Return each employee name and their manager's name as manager_name. Employees without a manager must still appear, with NULL.

checks.label: joins employees to itself with an outer join
matches manager_id to the manager row id

questions.explanation: An INNER JOIN would silently drop the top-level employee. A RIGHT JOIN with the aliases swapped is equivalent. Verified on PostgreSQL with 8 sample rows.

questions.prompt: Tables departments(id, name) and employees(id, dept_id), where some employees have dept_id NULL. Return the names of departments that have no employees.

checks.label: uses NOT EXISTS or a LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL anti-join

questions.model:
SELECT d.name
FROM departments d
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM employees e WHERE e.dept_id = d.id);
questions.explanation: NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees) is the tempting version, but the NULL dept_id makes it return no rows at all. Both NOT EXISTS and LEFT JOIN ... IS NULL are safe.

questions.prompt: Query: SELECT d.name, e.name FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id WHERE e.salary > 100. A teammate expected departments without any high earner to appear with NULLs. What actually happens?

options.text: They vanish, since NULL > 100 is unknown; move the salary test into ON.
options.why: Right: a WHERE filter on the right table silently turns the LEFT JOIN into an inner join.

options.text: The planner rewrites the LEFT JOIN into a FULL JOIN to preserve the unmatched departments.
options.why: Planners only rewrite outer joins into inner joins when it is safe, never the other way.

options.text: The query fails because a LEFT JOIN may only be filtered in HAVING, never in WHERE.
options.why: WHERE is allowed; it is just applied after the join.

options.text: Every department appears, and rows with salary of 100 or less show NULL in the name column.
options.why: WHERE removes whole rows; it never nulls individual columns.

questions.explanation: ON decides which right rows match; WHERE decides which result rows survive. For outer joins, conditions on the optional side belong in ON (or use IS NULL OR ... deliberately).

questions.prompt: A LEFT JOIN can return more rows than the left table contains.

options.why: Right: when a left row matches several right rows it appears once per match.
It can: a one-to-many match repeats the left row for each right row.

questions.explanation: A LEFT JOIN guarantees at least one row per left row, not at most one. That fan-out is why SUM() over a joined parent column double counts.

questions.prompt: Select all true statements about the logical evaluation order of a SELECT query.

options.text: FROM and JOIN are evaluated before WHERE.
options.why: Right: rows are produced, then filtered.

options.text: WHERE is evaluated before GROUP BY, so it cannot filter on aggregates.
options.why: Right: that is why HAVING exists.

options.text: ORDER BY can refer to a column alias defined in the SELECT list.
options.why: Right: ORDER BY runs after SELECT in the logical order.

options.text: A SELECT alias can be used in the WHERE clause of the same query.
options.why: WHERE runs before SELECT is evaluated, so PostgreSQL rejects the alias.

options.text: HAVING is evaluated before GROUP BY.
options.why: HAVING filters groups, so it runs after GROUP BY.

questions.explanation: Logical order: FROM/JOIN, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, window functions, SELECT, DISTINCT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. The optimiser may execute differently but must return the same result.
